A monogenic<ref name="ency_math">{{cite web |title=Monogenic function |url=http://encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php?title=Monogenic_function&oldid=47887 |website=Encyclopedia of Math |access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref><ref name='wolfram_math'>{{cite web |title=Monogenic Function|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/MonogenicFunction.html |website=Wolfram MathWorld |access-date=15 January 2021}}</ref> function is a [[complex function]] with a single finite [[Complex derivative|derivative]]. 
More precisely, a function <math> f(z) </math> defined on <math>A \subseteq \mathbb{C}</math> is called monogenic at <math> \zeta \in A </math>, if <math> f'(\zeta) </math> exists and is finite, with:
<math display="block">f'(\zeta) = \lim_{z\to\zeta}\frac{f(z) - f(\zeta)}{z - \zeta}</math>

Alternatively, it can be defined as the above [[Limit of a function|limit]] having the same value for all paths. Functions can either have a single derivative (monogenic) or infinitely many derivatives (polygenic), with no intermediate cases.<ref name="wolfram_math"/> Furthermore, a function <math> f(x) </math> which is monogenic <math> \forall \zeta \in B </math>, is said to be monogenic on <math> B </math>, and if <math> B </math> is a [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]] of <math> \mathbb{C}</math>, then it is [[Analytic function|analytic]] as well (The notion of domains can also be generalized <ref name='ency_math'/> in a manner such that functions which are monogenic over non-connected subsets of <math> \mathbb{C} </math>, can show a weakened form of analyticity)

The term monogenic was coined by [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy|Cauchy]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=A history of analysis |date=2003 |publisher=American Mathematical Society; London Mathematical Society |isbn=978-0-8218-2623-2 |editor-last=Jahnke |editor-first=H. N. |series=History of mathematics |location=Providence, RI : [London] |page=229}}</ref>
